description: Redbone's irresistible funk-rock plea — the first top-five hit by a Native American band — finally got an official music video in 2020, an animated short in a Native ledger-art style, decades after Guardians of the Galaxy turned it into Peter Quill's signature groove.

pops.text: The song started out as a promotional track under a different title: 'Hail.'
It was written by guitarist Lolly Vegas, who produced it together with his brother Pat, the band's bassist.
It first appeared on the band's fifth album, Wovoka, in 1973; the single followed in January 1974.
The hit single runs 3:27, but the album version stretches to 5:02, with a slow intro and a longer coda.
Lolly Vegas doubles on electric sitar, and the session players include Joe Sample on piano and vibraphone and orchestrator Gene Page.
Brothers Pat and Lolly were born with the surname Vasquez and renamed themselves Vegas on manager Bumps Blackwell's advice; 'Redbone' is a Cajun term for a person of mixed race.
It peaked at No. 5 on the Billboard Hot 100 on April 13, 1974 — the first top-five single ever by a Native American band.
The record spent 23 weeks on the Hot 100, 18 of them in the Top 40, and finished at No. 4 on Billboard's year-end chart for 1974.
The band performed it on The Midnight Special on February 22, 1974, introduced by a traditional Native American dance.
Guardians of the Galaxy (2014) revived it as the song on Peter Quill's mixtape — the soundtrack album hit No. 1 on the Billboard 200 — and it later became the theme song of Netflix's F Is for Family.

title: Come and Get Your Love

description: Bowie ditches glam for 'plastic soul' — this is his electric performance of the title track on The Dick Cavett Show in December 1974, months before the album landed.

pops.text: You're watching Bowie on The Dick Cavett Show, December 4, 1974 — gaunt, cane in hand, debuting his new soul direction on American TV.
He recorded the song in August 1974 at Sigma Sound in Philadelphia, chasing the Philly soul sound of Gamble and Huff.
Sessions began days after Richard Nixon resigned — hence the lyric 'Do you remember President Nixon?' dropped into the middle.
Hear those backing vocals? One of the singers is a then-unknown 23-year-old named Luther Vandross, who also arranged them.
Vandross's own song 'Funky Music (Is a Part of Me)' was reworked by Bowie into 'Fascination' on the same album.
The honking saxophone is David Sanborn, years before he became a smooth-jazz star in his own right.
Guitarist Carlos Alomar joined on this album and stayed in Bowie's band for decades — one of his longest collaborations.
Bowie called the album's style 'plastic soul' — 'the squashed remains of ethnic music... written and sung by a white limey.'
Released as a single in February 1975, it reached #28 on the Billboard Hot 100 — his biggest US hit yet at that point.
The same album sessions later produced 'Fame,' co-written with John Lennon — Bowie's first American #1.

title: Young Americans

description: The third smash single from Kick, with Richard Lowenstein's strobe-happy video filmed in and on Prague's ornate Municipal House.

pops.text: That flashing imagery isn't your screen glitching — the original broadcast carried an epilepsy warning for its strobe effects.
Director Richard Lowenstein filmed the band in Prague's Municipal House, an art-nouveau palace — the performance footage is on its roof and balcony.
Andrew Farriss wrote the music and Michael Hutchence the words — the partnership behind nearly every INXS hit.
It's from Kick (1987), produced by Chris Thomas and recorded in Sydney and Paris.
Kick was a hit machine: 'Need You Tonight,' 'Devil Inside,' 'New Sensation' and 'Never Tear Us Apart' all reached the US top 10.
This one peaked at #3 on the Billboard Hot 100 in the summer of 1988 — and only #25 in the UK, where INXS always lagged behind.
Kirk Pengilly's saxophone threads through the track — INXS kept a sax player in the lineup long after it stopped being fashionable.
Kick went on to sell more than 20 million copies worldwide and made the Sydney band global headliners.
Lowenstein directed most of the Kick-era videos, giving the campaign a consistent, high-gloss look across four singles.
Three years later the band played Wembley Stadium to 74,000 people — the Live Baby Live show — with this song in the set.

title: New Sensation

description: Zeppelin never played this Tolkien-haunted Led Zeppelin II gem live in their heyday — this is the first complete performance, at the 2007 O2 Arena reunion with Jason Bonham on drums.

pops.text: Historic footage: this December 10, 2007 O2 Arena show was the first time Led Zeppelin ever played 'Ramble On' in full, live.
In the '70s the band only teased fragments of it inside 'Whole Lotta Love' — the layered studio track was too tricky to reproduce on stage.
It was recorded in 1969 at Juggy Sound Studio in New York, in the middle of the band's second American tour.
Robert Plant's lyrics dive straight into Tolkien: Mordor, Gollum, and 'the evil one' who crept up and slipped away with her.
Plant was 21 when he sang this. In later years he admitted to cringing a little at his Lord of the Rings phase.
John Paul Jones's melodic bass line carries the verses — his playing is the quiet engine of the whole track.
The song was never released as a single in the US or UK in the 20th century — it became a classic purely as an album track.
Led Zeppelin II knocked the Beatles' Abbey Road off the top of the US chart and has sold over 12 million copies in America alone.
Behind the kit here is Jason Bonham, son of drummer John Bonham, whose death in 1980 had ended the band.
Roughly 20 million people applied for tickets to this one-off Ahmet Ertegun tribute show — for an arena holding fewer than 20,000.

title: Ramble On

description: Sting's reggae-rock tale of heartbreak from Outlandos d'Amour — the video finds the band lip-syncing their way through Tokyo's trains and streets in 1980.

pops.text: The video was shot guerrilla-style in Tokyo in 1980, while the band toured Japan — platforms, trains and crosswalks as the set.
Sting openly based the song on Bob Marley's 'No Woman, No Cry' — he borrowed its spirit and phrasing, then flipped it into a lament.
It was the third single from the debut album Outlandos d'Amour, first released on November 24, 1978 — and it went nowhere.
The album was recorded at Surrey Sound Studios on a shoestring — around £1,500 borrowed from manager Miles Copeland.
Miles was drummer Stewart Copeland's brother. He later founded I.R.S. Records; at this point he was funding the band out of pocket.
Notice the edit: the single and video run 3:10, while the album version stretches to 4:50 with extra guitar workouts.
Andy Summers's clipped, chorused guitar stabs are pure reggae rhythm playing — filtered through a punk band's impatience.
Re-released in February 1980, after 'Roxanne' and 'Can't Stand Losing You' had broken through, it finally climbed to #6 in the UK.
Watch Sting mug into a walkie-talkie like a microphone — the band turned the travel footage into a running visual gag.
The title of the parent album is a mangled-French pun: 'Outlandos d'Amour' — outlaws of love.

title: So Lonely

description: The slinky, after-midnight groove that became Petty's first hit — track two of the 1976 debut album, built around a guitar lick the band re-cut the whole song to feature.

pops.text: That hypnotic guitar figure is Mike Campbell's. The song existed without it — until one very long night in the studio.
The band first cut a seven-minute version. Near the end, Campbell idly played this lick — and visiting songwriter Dwight Twilley yelled, 'That's the lick!'
Petty stopped the tape, called the band — who had all gone home — and they returned around 2:30 in the morning to re-cut the song around it.
Campbell nearly played the riff with a slide — he experimented with a ridged pill bottle — before deciding it sounded too bluesy.
The final edit is a tight 2:43. Benmont Tench's Fender Rhodes piano gives it that smoky, late-night sway.
Dwight Twilley Band singer Phil Seymour helps out on backing vocals — Shelter Records labelmates returning the favor.
Released as a single in 1977, it stiffed — then a re-release after months of touring cracked the Top 40, peaking at #40.
It was Petty's first single and first hit. Producer Denny Cordell's Shelter Records had bet on a Gainesville bar band.
The song turned up in the 1978 film FM — the radio-station movie that helped inspire the sitcom WKRP in Cincinnati.
Grace Jones covered it in 1980 as a reggae track on Warm Leatherette — proof the groove travels anywhere.

title: Breakdown

description: Prince and Apollonia's Purple Rain duet, performed here live in Houston in January 1985 on the Purple Rain tour — the official video the Prince estate finally released to YouTube in 2017.

pops.text: This is the official live video: Houston, January 1985, mid-Purple Rain tour — Prince in full imperial purple pomp.
On the record it's a duet with Apollonia Kotero. On stage, Wendy Melvoin and Lisa Coleman take her vocal lines.
The song was originally meant for Apollonia 6's album — and before that, for Vanity, who quit Prince's camp just before Purple Rain filming.
When Vanity left, Prince recast the role with Patricia 'Apollonia' Kotero and renamed the group around her.
Prince recorded the track at Sunset Sound in Los Angeles in January 1984, writing it for the film's motorcycle-ride scene.
Those opening finger cymbals and strings give it a psychedelic shimmer unlike anything else on the Purple Rain soundtrack.
Released in January 1985, it was the fifth and final US single from Purple Rain, reaching #25 on the Hot 100.
Its B-side was another Purple Rain showpiece: 'Baby I'm a Star.'
While Prince lived, he kept his videos off YouTube entirely. His estate only posted the Purple Rain clips in 2017, with the deluxe reissue.
Purple Rain — album and film — made 1984 Prince's year: the LP spent 24 straight weeks at #1.

title: Take Me with U

description: Achtung Baby's funkiest single, with Stéphane Sednaoui's distorted, belly-dancer-starring video shot in Morocco — the moment U2 learned to groove.

pops.text: Director Stéphane Sednaoui shot this in Fez, Morocco, warping the band with distorting lenses while a belly dancer swirls through the frame.
The dancer is Morleigh Steinberg. She later joined the Zoo TV tour — and in 2002 she married The Edge.
The song grew from a discarded demo called 'Sick Puppy.' The band salvaged Adam Clayton's bass line and rebuilt everything around it.
The Edge's wah-drenched guitar came through a Korg A3 effects unit — a once-cheap box that fans have hunted down ever since to copy the sound.
It was recorded between Hansa Tonstudio in Berlin and Dublin, with producers Daniel Lanois and Brian Eno pushing the band to reinvent themselves.
Achtung Baby was U2's Berlin record — made in a reunified Germany while the band argued so bitterly they nearly split.
Released December 2, 1991 as the album's second single, it hit #9 on the Hot 100.
On Billboard's Modern Rock Tracks it ruled for nine weeks — at the time, the longest-running #1 in that chart's history.
Bono's lyric sends 'Johnny' walking 'with your sister the moon' — one of the album's many tangles of the spiritual and the sensual.
Live on Zoo TV, Steinberg's dance became a set-piece — The Fly-era U2 embracing spectacle they'd once have run from.

title: Mysterious Ways

description: Reid Genauer performs his song "Honest Hour" solo on acoustic guitar in this 2006 video — the Strangefolk co-founder showcasing the tune that later anchored Assembly of Dust's live album The Honest Hour.

pops.text: Assembly of Dust formed in 2002 around Reid Genauer, co-founder and frontman of the Vermont jam band Strangefolk, which he had left in 2001.
Genauer named the band after his 2003 solo album, which was also called Assembly of Dust.
'Honest Hour' is the title track of the band's 2004 live album The Honest Hour, released that September on Hybrid Recordings.
The album was recorded live at Revolution Hall in Troy, New York, in February 2004; other performances from the same February 21 show were released 20 years later as The Promised Hour.
Genauer approached the live record 'as if we were playing a studio album live,' and the crowd noise was cleaned up so the album plays almost like a studio recording.
The album's nine songs mix brand-new Assembly of Dust material with reimagined versions of songs Genauer wrote for Strangefolk.
The quintet on the record: Genauer on vocals and guitar, Nate Wilson on keyboards, Adam Terrell on lead guitar, John Leccese on bass and Andy Herrick on drums.
The Home Grown Music Network called the title track the album's finest moment — an introspection on a man's final 'honest hour' over a soft, true-country shuffle and gorgeous harmonies.
The band's cited influences run to Steely Dan, The Band, J.J. Cale and Little Feat, and its rootsy groove has been dubbed 'hick funk.'
The song kept a long live afterlife: it appears as track 6 on the band's official live release Found Sound II (2014), recorded in 2013 at Infinity Hall in Norfolk, Connecticut.

title: Honest Hour

description: The duo's sixth and final #1 — Jeff Stein's surreal video traps Hall and Oates inside a giant bass drum before spelling the title out in building-sized letters.

pops.text: Yes, the video opens with Hall and Oates trapped inside an enormous bass drum while their band plays on without them.
Director Jeff Stein also made Tom Petty's 'Don't Come Around Here No More' — a connoisseur of comically oversized visuals.
Hall later noted his leopard-print suit in this clip 'made me look like a Dalmatian.'
It's the lead single from Big Bam Boom (1984), the album where the duo leaned hard into drum machines and dance production.
Dance remixer Arthur Baker was brought in as a consultant, giving their blue-eyed soul a club-ready electronic edge.
The song topped the Billboard Hot 100 for two weeks in December 1984 — the duo's sixth #1 single.
It was also their last #1. Their run made them the most successful duo in US chart history, passing the Everly Brothers.
Hall and Oates wrote it together — a rarity balance in a partnership where Hall usually took the songwriting lead.
In 2004 the song got a second life when Uniting Nations' dance cover became a UK top-10 hit.
Gamers know it too: it blasts from the Flash FM speakers in Grand Theft Auto: Vice City's neon 1986 Miami.

title: Out of Touch

description: Doolittle's sunniest single — the band mocks the very idea of a music video, miming through a fisheye lens with their mouths hanging open instead of lip-syncing.

pops.text: Black Francis wrote this song when he was about fourteen — years before the Pixies existed.
The band thought it was too poppy. An earlier version was cut in their 1987 demo sessions and left off Surfer Rosa.
Producer Gil Norton championed it for Doolittle, recorded at Carriage House Studios in Stamford, Connecticut.
Francis said the lyric is about hobos riding the rails in California — and dying in an earthquake. Sunny song, dark subject.
Joey Santiago's chiming, surf-tinged guitar riff is the hook — one of the most imitated sounds in indie rock.
Notice the video trick: Francis and Kim Deal open and shut their mouths in time but never form the words — a deliberate anti-lip-sync.
Francis called the clip's theme 'water on the brain.' Directors Neil Pollock and Jonathan Bekemeier shot it through a distorting fisheye lens.
Released as a single in June 1989, it reached #3 on Billboard's Modern Rock Tracks — the Pixies' biggest US chart showing of their first era.
In the UK it only managed #54, but Doolittle itself became one of the defining albums of the alternative era.
Decades later it remains the Pixies song most likely to be playing in a movie — including a memorable spot in (500) Days of Summer.

title: Here Comes Your Man

description: The Cars' purest dance-floor command — the title track of their 1981 album, and an early-MTV staple from the years when the channel and the band grew up together.

pops.text: Ric Ocasek had actually written this one years earlier — the band finally cut it for the 1981 album that shares its name.
Shake It Up was the first Cars album recorded at Syncro Sound, the Boston studio the band bought for themselves.
Producer Roy Thomas Baker — of Queen fame — returned to polish their new-wave sheen one more time.
Greg Hawkes's bouncing synthesizer riff drives the track — the Cars treated keyboards as a lead instrument from day one.
Ocasek, who sings lead here, said the lyric is exactly what it sounds like: an instruction to get on the dance floor.
Unlike most Cars hits sung by bassist Benjamin Orr, this is an Ocasek vocal — drier, twitchier, unmistakably his.
The single peaked at #4 on the Billboard Hot 100 in early 1982 and #2 on the Mainstream Rock chart.
The video, directed by Paul Justman, became an early MTV staple — the channel had launched just months before the album.
On the dance chart, the single was billed as a double-sided entry: 'Shake It Up / Cruiser,' its B-side album mate.
The album marked a pop pivot from Panorama's moody experiments — the title track was the band pointing back at the charts.

title: Shake It Up

description: Bernie Taupin's California love letter from Madman Across the Water — this official video only arrived in 2017, when Max Weiland's film of a dozen Los Angeles drivers won Elton's 'The Cut' competition.

pops.text: For 46 years this song had no official video. This one premiered at Cannes in 2017, made by Max Weiland for Elton's 'The Cut' filmmaker competition.
The video follows a dozen Los Angeles drivers — a nod to the song's California origins, all unfolding behind the wheel.
Bernie Taupin wrote the lyric about his first wife, Maxine Feibelman — the 'seamstress for the band' who really did sew patches onto their jeans.
Taupin was inspired by his first trip to California in 1970 — the women there seemed, to a lad from rural Lincolnshire, like another species.
It opens Madman Across the Water, recorded at the Château d'Hérouville studio in France in 1971.
Paul Buckmaster's sweeping string arrangement lifts the final choruses — his orchestrations were Elton's early-career secret weapon.
At over six minutes, it was long for a single. Released in the US in 1972, it stalled at #41 — and wasn't a UK single at all.
A pre-Yes Rick Wakeman was among the session players on the album, adding keyboards before prog stardom called.
The bus singalong in Cameron Crowe's Almost Famous (2000) resurrected it — a whole generation learned the chorus from that scene.
Rolling Stone's 2021 list of the 500 greatest songs placed 'Tiny Dancer' at #47 — not bad for a #41 single.

title: Tiny Dancer

description: Phish's wordless adrenaline shot, seen here in pro-shot footage from their Riviera Maya, Mexico run on February 24, 2023 — Trey Anastasio's guitar-heroics closer in full flight.

pops.text: This pro-shot performance comes from Phish's Riviera Maya run in Mexico, February 24, 2023 — the song opening the second set.
Trey Anastasio wrote it with his solo band's rhythm section: bassist Tony Markellis and drummer Russ Lawton.
It debuted on April 17, 1998 at Higher Ground in Winooski, Vermont — the one and only show by a one-off group called 8 Foot Fluorescent Tubes.
That first version had vocals, sung by Heloise Williams. Phish's version is a pure instrumental — and stayed that way.
Phish premiered their take on September 9, 1999, opening night of fall tour at GM Place in Vancouver.
The studio version landed on Farmhouse (2000), recorded at The Barn — Anastasio's converted Vermont studio.
Watch for the peak: Trey raises his guitar skyward and lets it feed back in a pose fans call his 'Jedi' moment.
Some versions turn the arena into a trampoline — the December 2009 Madison Square Garden performance famously had the whole crowd bouncing in unison.
It's a set-closer and encore weapon: no lyrics, no balladry, just a riff engineered to detonate a room.
The song also lives a double life in the Trey Anastasio Band, where its writers Markellis and Lawton anchor the groove.

title: First Tube

description: The closing track of No Jacket Required — a world-touring video for a song that sounds like a homecoming anthem but is sung from inside a locked ward.

pops.text: Listen to the backing chant of 'take me home' — those voices belong to Sting and Peter Gabriel, plus singer Helen Terry.
Gabriel was Collins's old Genesis bandmate; his leaving the band in 1975 is what put Collins behind the microphone in the first place.
It isn't really about going home. Collins has said the lyric is a mental-institution patient's plea, inspired by One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest.
The video hops between world cities — London, New York, Tokyo, Sydney among them — shot around his touring life.
It closes No Jacket Required (1985), the album that turned Collins into the defining pop sound of the decade.
That album won the Grammy for Album of the Year and sold some 25 million copies.
Released as a UK single in July 1985 it reached #19; in the US it climbed to #7 in 1986.
Collins plays his own drums throughout — the gated, thunderous kit sound he pioneered remained his trademark.
From the No Jacket Required tour onward, this became his traditional show-closer — the last song of the night, almost every night.
In 2003 Bone Thugs-N-Harmony sampled it for their single 'Home' — and Collins, charmed, flew in to appear in their video.

title: Take Me Home
